title: Java OOP Quick Revision: Classes to equals/hashCode
summary: Night-before revision notes on Java classes, constructors, access modifiers, static, final, inheritance, abstract classes vs interfaces, overloading vs overriding, and the equals/hashCode contract.

chapters.title: Classes and Objects Mental Model
points: Class is a blueprint; `new` allocates an object on the heap and the variable holds a reference, not the object
Fields get defaults (0, false, null) but local variables do not: using an unassigned local is a compile error
`this` refers to the current object; use it to resolve name shadowing (`this.name = name`) and to chain constructors with `this(...)`
Assigning one reference to another (`b = a`) copies the reference, so both point to the same object; `==` compares references
Interview Point: What is the difference between a class and an object? Where do objects live in memory? What does `==` compare for objects? What are the default values of fields vs locals?

chapters.title: Constructors and Initialization Order
points: Constructor has the class name and no return type; if you write none, the compiler adds a default no-arg constructor
Writing any constructor removes the default one, so `new Foo()` then fails to compile unless you declare it

Every constructor calls `super(...)` or `this(...)`, traditionally as its first statement (Java 25 allows earlier statements that do not use `this`); the implicit `super()` fails if the parent has no no-arg constructor
Init order: static blocks (once, at class load) → parent fields/initializer blocks → parent constructor → child fields/initializer blocks → child constructor
Calling an overridable method from a constructor is a bug: the child override runs before child fields are initialized

Interview Point: When does the compiler give a default constructor? Can a constructor be private, and why (singleton)? In what order do parent and child initialize? Can constructors be inherited or overridden?

chapters.title: Access Modifiers, static and final
points: Visibility widest to narrowest: `public` (everywhere) > `protected` (same package + subclasses) > package-private (no keyword, same package) > `private` (same class only)
`static` members belong to the class, not an instance: shared across all objects, accessed as `ClassName.member`, and a static method cannot use `this` or instance fields directly
`final` variable is assigned once; a `final` reference can't be reassigned but the object it points to can still be mutated
`final` method cannot be overridden and `final` class cannot be extended (`String` is final); `static` methods are hidden, not overridden
Constants are `public static final` with UPPER_CASE names; static blocks run once when the class loads
Interview Point: Difference between protected and package-private? Does final make an object immutable? Can a static method be overridden? Why is String final?

chapters.title: Inheritance, Abstract Classes and Interfaces
points: `extends` gives single class inheritance; `super.method()` calls the parent version and `super(...)` calls the parent constructor; private members are not inherited
Abstract class: may hold state, constructors, and both abstract and concrete methods; cannot be instantiated; a class extends only one
Interface: a contract with no instance state (only constants); a class can `implements` many; methods are public abstract by default, plus `default` and `static` methods since Java 8
Pick abstract class for shared state and partial implementation in an is-a family; pick interface for a capability across unrelated classes
Diamond problem: if two interfaces give the same default method, the class must override it and may pick one with `A.super.m()`

Interview Point: Abstract class vs interface, when to use each? Why can't Java extend multiple classes but can implement multiple interfaces? Can an abstract class have a constructor? Can an interface have a method body?

chapters.title: Overloading vs Overriding and equals/hashCode
points: Overloading: same name, different parameter list (return type alone is not enough), resolved at compile time by the declared argument types

Overriding: same signature in a subclass, resolved at runtime by the actual object type (dynamic dispatch); use `@Override`, return type may be covariant, access cannot be narrowed, and it cannot throw broader checked exceptions
Default `equals` is reference equality (`==`); override it to compare state: check `this == o`, check null/class, cast, then compare fields (use `Objects.equals`)
Contract: equal objects must return the same `hashCode`; the reverse is not required, and `hashCode` must be consistent across calls; use `Objects.hash(fields)`
Overriding `equals` without `hashCode` breaks `HashMap` and `HashSet`: the object is not found because it lands in a different bucket; never use mutable fields in the hash of a key

Interview Point: Overloading vs overriding, which is compile-time? What is the equals/hashCode contract? What happens if you override only equals? Why does `equals(Object)` with the wrong parameter type only overload instead of override?

chapters.title: Java OOP Cheat Sheet
points: Modifier table: private < package-private < protected < public, and which scopes each reaches
Keyword effects: `static` = class-level, `final` variable = no reassign, `final` method = no override, `final` class = no extend, `abstract` = no instantiate
Abstract class vs interface table: state, constructors, multiple inheritance, default methods, use case
Overloading = compile time / overriding = runtime; always annotate with `@Override`
equals/hashCode recipe: `this == o` → class check → cast → `Objects.equals` fields; hash with `Objects.hash` of the same fields; override both or neither
Interview Point: Which two rules would you recite for a correct equals/hashCode? What are the init-order steps? Which keyword combination is illegal (abstract + final, abstract + private/static)?
